ruling: E1 should be ruled for v5 (the journal is the authority), with conditions attached. The case for keeping v1 does not survive contact with v1's own code. In v1, the structure that decides what exists is the in-memory vector index. A deposit becomes durable only at the next sleep-pass snapshot, and the attention WAL calls flush() but never fsync, even though the docstring at src/moneta/api.py:417 says "fsync'd to the WAL" (the code is at src/moneta/durability.py:149). Every risk I found in v5 comes from this implementation, not from making the journal authoritative. The one design-level cost is that the journal grows without bound and open replays all of it. That has a standard fix: a checkpoint.
strongest_case_for_v1: v1's protocol has two structures and two rules (USD first, then the vector index; the index is authoritative). It is short, it was locked through Rounds 2 and 3, and the Phase 2 and Phase 3 envelope was measured against it. Its crash story is closed-form: an interrupted write leaves a USD orphan that Pcp never traverses, so healing is implicit and needs no recovery code. v5 adds a third persistent structure plus a set of recovery mechanisms: torn-tail truncation, CRC refusal, repair(), quarantine files, sha sidecars, snapshot reconciliation, revector-from-snapshot and a failed-migration rename. Each one is new code that can be wrong at the worst moment. v5 also puts an fsync on every write, including signal_attention, which v1 kept off the hot path. And it ties open time and file size to total history instead of the live set. Finally, SYNAPSE runs today on v1's failure semantics; 6 of its tests pin them as the contract. A cutover that changes the substrate's source of truth under a production consumer is a bigger risk than the data losses v1 has already shown.
concrete_risks_in_v5_code: Hard crash during v1 to v5 migration leaves a store that cannot open, and the error's suggested fix silently loses memories (probed, Windows, Python 3.14). (1) Whether to migrate is decided only by whether the journal file exists (src/moneta/v5/compat.py:416). (2) The migration note and sidecar hash are written only at the very end (compat.py:656-659). (3) The .failed-migration rename (compat.py:446) runs only on an in-process exception, and tests/v5/test_compat.py:191 tests only that path. Result: os._exit after 1, 20 or 52 of 52 appends all reopen with SnapshotDivergedError ('written by another writer', compat.py:217-223, :250). Following the message's first fix, 'Move the snapshot aside to continue', on the 20-append case opened with 19 of 50 records, and close() then exported that 19-record set over snapshot.json. snapshot.json.v1-original (compat.py:560-562) still holds the data, so it is recoverable, but only by an operator who knows to look for it.

A complete but damaged final line refuses the whole store (probed). A torn tail without a newline is truncated (src/moneta/v5/journal.py:119-121), but a final line whose CRC fails, such as a sector tear that kept the trailing newline, raises JournalCorruptError at open (journal.py:124-127). Probe: zeroing 20 bytes of the last frame gave open refused. That record was never acknowledged, because fsync had not returned, so it would be safe to drop. Instead availability now depends on an operator running repair(). v1 in the same situation quarantines and keeps running.

The journal grows without bound and open replays all of it (design-level). The whole file is read into memory at open (journal.py:262). events() re-reads the whole file on any later call (journal.py:292-301), and compat._journal_known_shas runs it on every facade open whose snapshot hash is not in the sidecar (compat.py:181-191, :214). compact() scrubs only erased payloads and keeps every event (src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:910-941). Every signal_attention is a permanent event. Measured: 100k events = 29.4 MB and 0.81 s to open. That scales linearly with history, not with the live set, whereas v1's snapshot plus WAL truncation (durability.py:117-120) bounds replay.

Write cost and throughput ceiling (measured, Windows NVMe). fsync on every append (journal.py:326-327) costs 1.40 ms per deposit and 1.36 ms per signal_attention, against 0.043 ms and 0.012 ms with fsync=False. All writes are serialized under one RLock (substrate.py:297), so the ceiling is about 700 writes/s on this disk, lower on HDD or network storage. SYNAPSE gets the default (compat.Moneta fsync=True, compat.py:401) unless it changes code. This is the price of real durability, not a bug, but it moves attention onto the fsync path where v1 had none.

On Windows, run_sleep_pass raises after the pass is already committed (probed). With a reader holding snapshot.json open, os.replace fails with PermissionError WinError 5 (compat.py:99-107). The facade's run_sleep_pass then raises (compat.py:531-535) even though the retain and consolidate events are already journaled (seq 3 to 5 in the probe). close() swallows the same export failure (compat.py:499-510); run_sleep_pass does not. v1 uses the same os.replace (durability.py:109-116), so this is not a regression, but under v5 a failure of a derived file is reported as a failure of the operation.

A crash between USD projection and the consolidate event re-projects the same records. The projection runs at substrate.py:708 and is journaled only at substrate.py:719-727. After a kill in between, the records are still STAGED and are projected again on the next pass (substrate.py:694). UsdTarget writes to /Memory_{hex} (src/moneta/usd_target.py:163-165) in a sublayer chosen by UTC date (usd_target.py:271-280). A retry on the same day overwrites the same prim; a retry on a later day defines a duplicate prim in a second sublayer and inflates _prim_counts, which feeds rotation. v1's argument that orphans are benign (ARCHITECTURE.md §7) was made for unreferenced prims under index authority. It does not automatically cover duplicate defs, and this is §9 Trigger 3 territory.

Lock-sidecar and in-process registry edge cases. Exclusivity is msvcrt.locking on byte 0 of <journal>.lock (journal.py:143-150). The facade also keeps v1's URI registry (compat.py:405-409). Two different storage_uri values that share one snapshot_path now fail with JournalLockedError instead of silently sharing; that is better behavior but a new exception type for SYNAPSE. Behavior on network shares (SMB byte-range locks) is untested.

Not a risk, for calibration: exporting snapshot.json on every add, which SYNAPSE does until cutover step 3, is cheaper on v5 than on v1. At 841 records, dim 64: v1 46.7 ms vs v5 30.4 ms per add. At dim 768: 422.8 ms vs 231.2 ms.
conditions_to_attach_if_ruled_for_v5: Make migration crash-safe before cutover step 2. Journal a migration_begin event (with the snapshot sha256 and the expected row count) immediately after genesis and before the first import. On open, a journal that has migration_begin but no completion note is a half-migrated journal: re-migrate from snapshot.json.v1-original, or rename it to .failed-migration, and never treat it as authoritative. Change the SnapshotDivergedError text so it does not offer 'move the snapshot aside' first when a migration is incomplete. Add a hard-kill test (os._exit at several points during migration) next to tests/v5/test_compat.py:191.

Treat a CRC-failing final line as a torn tail, logged and quarantined automatically, because a record that was never fsync-acknowledged was never promised. Keep the hard JournalCorruptError for damage in the middle of the file.

Bound open cost: add a checkpoint/fold-snapshot event, or a derived fold cache keyed by seq and hash, so open replays only the tail after it. Stop _journal_known_shas from scanning the whole journal on every open. Set a stated budget, for example 'open of a 1-year SYNAPSE store under N seconds', and measure against it.

Decide and document the attention durability tier: fsync each signal_attention (current), or group-commit attention while deposits stay fsync'd. Record the measured per-op cost (about 1.4 ms on NVMe) in BEHAVIOR_CHANGES so SYNAPSE knows the write ceiling.

Facade: make run_sleep_pass treat failure of the derived v1 export the same way close() does (log, record in SleepPassResult or a journal note, do not raise), because the pass is already committed. Document the Windows behavior when snapshot.json is held open by a reader.

Make re-projection after a crash between project and consolidate idempotent across sublayer days (route a retried id back to its original sublayer, or record the target layer in a journaled project-intent event before projecting). Brief it as §9 Trigger 3 if it touches the §15.2 envelope.

Record in the ruling that v1's existing durability claim is false: src/moneta/api.py:417 says signals are fsync'd, but src/moneta/durability.py:149 only flushes. This corrects the record and is one of the factual grounds for E1.

Keep the cutover discipline in docs/v5/BLUEPRINT.md §9: rehearse on a copy of the 841-record 17 Sep store and read the migration report; move hython and the server Python together; keep the v1-format export as the rollback path until 5.0.0 has run on SYNAPSE in production for an agreed period.
Caveat on the evidence: the Jev triage's question state came from v5's own blueprint. Rest the ruling on the code findings above, not on the 1.0 settle score.
recommendation: Rule E1 for v5, conditionally. The decisive fact is that v1's authority for "what exists" is a structure that cannot survive process death, and its WAL does not fsync even though the docstring says it does (src/moneta/api.py:417 vs src/moneta/durability.py:149). v5's journal is the only fsync'd, checksummed structure, and the core of its implementation is sound. That rests on: torn-tail truncation (probed OK); append rollback on a failed write (journal.py:328-340); poisoning on fold failure (substrate.py:425-437); and per-add export cheaper than v1's. Do not move to cutover step 2 (pointing SYNAPSE at the facade) until the migration crash window is closed, because that is the one path where following v5's own error message loses data. Bounding replay with a checkpoint can come before 5.0.0. The other conditions are polish. Probe scripts are in C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-User-Moneta\eb45e56e-ffee-4251-86c6-41782cf26935\scratchpad\e1 (probe1.py, mk_v1.py, crash_mig.py, reopen.py, replace_probe.py, export_probe.py). No repo files were edited.

ruling: E2 for v5, with conditions. My skeptic case holds on the math but not on the decision. With a memoryless exponential, "mutate at three points" and "evaluate purely from an anchor" give the same numbers. I measured a relative drift of 3.7e-13 across 10k compounded v1-style mutations against one v5 exp. So E2 does nothing a one-line v1 reorder couldn't for correctness. What decides it is E1/I1/I6: once the journal is authoritative and live state must equal replay (substrate.py:425-437 journal-then-fold; tests/v5/test_conformance.py:274 test_i6_reads_never_write), a read cannot write. Otherwise every query has to journal (an fsync on the read path), or live state drifts from replay. E2 therefore follows from E1 and is not a separate choice. If E1 is ruled for v5, E2 has to come with it. If E1 falls, E2 doesn't matter. On clock faults v5 is also the safer design: a forward clock spike under v1 permanently over-decays and freezes every row, while under v5 it touches only the ids attended during the spike.
strongest_case_for_v1: The decay is memoryless, so v1's write-back at three points gives the same numbers as v5's pure anchor evaluation (measured drift 3.7e-13 over 10k mutations). E2 adds no correctness of its own. The real defect, P4 (attention reduce sets LastEvaluated=now and erases decay since the last query, ecs.py:212-247), can be fixed inside v1 by running decay_all(lam, now) before apply_attention. That is a §5 ordering amendment that keeps lock 2's three bounded, auditable mutation points. v1 also keeps two operational advantages: a native batched decay kernel on the read path (ecs.py:258-262, decay_batch), and a public runtime-tunable λ (api.py:210 self.decay, decay.py:91 set_half_life, per MONETA §2.3), which v5 drops in favour of close-and-reopen with history reinterpreted. Read-time purity also opens new surface in v5: caller-supplied evaluation times and event timestamps now decide the answer directly. The case fails because it only works if v1 keeps mutable snapshot state as truth. Under a journal-authoritative design, read-time mutation either has to be journaled or breaks replay.
concrete_risks_in_v5_code: Two copies of λ (latent split). Fold copies λ when it is constructed (src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:311 Fold(self._decay.lambda_)) and _op_attend uses that copy (src/moneta/v5/model.py:286). Reads use Substrate.lam = self._decay.lambda_ (substrate.py:388-389). Probe: calling s._decay.set_half_life(60) live, then reopening, gave live utility 4.3e-19 against replay 7.5e-37, so live state no longer equals replay. It needs private access today, but it becomes a real bug as soon as any runtime half-life setter is added.

Lost v1 surface for runtime decay tuning. v1 exposes m.decay (api.py:210; DecayConfig.set_half_life at decay.py:91) and m.ecs.decay_all (used at tests/integration/test_end_to_end_flow.py:407). compat.Moneta has no .decay attribute (probe: hasattr(compat.Moneta, 'decay') == False), and _EcsView (compat.py:324-355) has no decay_all. Any v1 caller that tunes λ live gets an AttributeError, a hard break. The only remaining path is reopening with a new half_life, which journals a note and reinterprets all history (substrate.py:328-350).

Forward clock spike freezes decay. Attend sets anchor_t = max(t, anchor_t) (model.py:289), and decay_value clamps negative dt to 0 (decay.py:66-68). Probe: an attend at T0+30d left utility frozen at its spiked value for every read at T0, T0+1d and T0+7d. Realistic trigger on Windows: w32time step corrections, sleep/resume, VM clock jumps (SystemClock is time.time(), substrate.py:103-105). The scope is narrower than v1's equivalent, which over-decays and re-stamps every row (ecs.py:251-272), but nothing in _t() (substrate.py:422-423) bounds or flags event times against the journal's high-water t.

Time-travel reads. Substrate.recall/explain accept any finite t (substrate.py:573-583, 422-423). Evaluating at a t earlier than an anchor returns the post-attend anchor value. Probe: utility 0.75 at T0+3600 when the true historical value was 0.5. This affects direct Substrate callers only, because compat.Moneta.query (compat.py:514) does not forward t, so SYNAPSE cannot reach it through the facade. `t` reads like an as-of query but is not one.

Read-path cost with no native decay seam. recall calls decay_value once per eligible record in Python (substrate.py:603; model.py:144-145). At N=50k, D=64 with v5 native cosines enabled: utility loop ~10ms, _classify ~38ms, cosines ~27ms, total recall ~111ms, against v1 query at 4.7ms with native decay_batch. Only about 10ms of that gap is E2. The rest is E1/policy classification. Still, v1 already has a bit-exact batched kernel that v5's read path does not use.

SYNAPSE semantic change. Memory.last_evaluated now means the evaluation time, not the last-mutation time (model.py:147-157 sets last_evaluated=t). SYNAPSE's crucible/fc4 helpers that write ecs._last_evaluated to fake elapsed time fail until they are re-pointed to record.anchor_t (docs/v5/SYNAPSE_COMPAT.md:37). Any consumer that reads last_evaluated as 'last touched' now always gets 'now'.

Migration carries P4 damage forward. migrate_v1 imports v1's stored (utility, last_evaluated) as the anchor unchanged (compat.py:598-619). Any decay that P4 already erased in a v1 snapshot is frozen into the v5 anchor and cannot be recovered. This is unavoidable, but it should be stated so nobody expects migrated utilities to be 'corrected'. Export writes the anchor pair back (compat.py:158-161), so round-trip to v1 is exact.
conditions_to_attach_if_ruled_for_v5: Rule E2 together with E1, not on its own. The ruling text should say that 'reads never write' follows from journal authority plus live==replay (I1/I6). It should also amend ARCHITECTURE.md §4: the formula stays verbatim, and 'three evaluation points' becomes 'zero mutation points; state changes only via journaled events (attend, retain)'.

One source of λ: Fold and Substrate must read the same value (fix substrate.py:311 vs 388-389). Add a test that any runtime λ change journals a half_life_change note and that live == replay afterwards.

Decide and document runtime λ tuning. Either add a journaled set_half_life to the harness surface (and a .decay shim on compat.Moneta) or state that tuning is reopen-only. v1's public m.decay / m.ecs.decay_all must not fail as an unexplained AttributeError.

Guard event timestamps. When an event's t is more than a bounded skew ahead of the journal's high-water t (or wall clock), warn and journal a note, or reject it. Add a test with a forward spike followed by a return to normal time.
Document that read-side `t` is evaluation time and not an as-of query, or reject t below the high-water anchor time for the records being evaluated.
Add the existing bit-exact native decay_batch seam to v5's read path (recall, run_sleep_pass, records) with a parity test, so E2 costs no more than v1's read-path decay.
Publish the Memory.last_evaluated semantic change in SYNAPSE_COMPAT.md and the API docs, and ask SYNAPSE to pass a clock instead of writing private time columns.

Keep the existing safeguards as invariants: retain events journal concrete prune/stage id lists (substrate.py:681-689), so a later λ reinterpretation can never retroactively un-prune or re-prune, and test_i6_reads_never_write stays mandatory.
recommendation: Rule E2 for v5, explicitly as a consequence of E1, and attach the conditions above before v5 becomes the default. In priority order: (1) one source of λ, (2) a decision on runtime half-life tuning with a compat shim or a documented break, (3) a timestamp skew guard on journaled events, (4) native decay on the v5 read path. If E1 is not ruled for v5, keep v1 lock 2 and fix P4 with a reorder in v1's reducer (decay_all before apply_attention in ecs.py:212-247 / the attention_log reducer), keeping the three mutation points. Do not take E2's Jev score (0.99) as independent support: the question state came from v5's own blueprint, and the substantive argument is E1's. All probes are in C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-User-Moneta\eb45e56e-ffee-4251-86c6-41782cf26935\scratchpad\e2\ (probe.py, bench.py, bench2.py). No repo files were edited.

ruling: E3 should go to v5, with conditions. The skeptic's case for v1 is right about one thing: v5 runs reads, writes, the sleep pass, USD projection and the compat snapshot export under a single substrate RLock. That gives up v1's 'readers never wait' property, and I measured that cost on this Windows machine. The case is wrong about correctness, and correctness is what E3 is ruling on. v1's 'lock-free' claim is already false once durability is on: wal_append takes a lock (src/moneta/durability.py:144) and only flushes, never fsyncs (durability.py:149), even though the api.py:416-418 docstring promises fsync. So acknowledged attention can be lost on crash. v1 is also locked to the GIL (attention_log.py:64-68), and its single-reducer rule is a convention the code does not enforce (attention_log.py:30-36). v5 gives a total order, durable attention, and live state equal to replay, and the tests check that (tests/v5/test_review_regressions.py:207-236, tests/v5/test_conformance.py:336-360). All 131 v5 tests pass on Windows when PYTHONPATH includes src. The real problems are lock scope and journal growth. Both can be fixed inside v5 and neither is a reason to keep the GIL log. Rule for v5 and attach the conditions below.
strongest_case_for_v1: v1's attention path costs about 0.23 us per signal: one list.append with no lock (src/moneta/attention_log.py:73). Query takes no lock at all (src/moneta/api.py:379-410), so an agent's read never waits behind a writer, a sleep pass or USD authoring. ARCHITECTURE.md:312 (section 15.6) narrowed the writer lock to the Sdf.ChangeBlock alone so that layer.Save() runs concurrently with readers. That narrowing was a hard-won Phase 2/3 envelope ruling, with a projected p95 reader stall of about 10-30 ms. Deferring attention to the sleep pass also gives a stable ranking within a session and one consolidation point. Immediate visibility brings a rich-get-richer feedback loop that SYNAPSE has never run against in production. The GIL dependency is not hidden: the constructor makes it fail loudly (attention_log.py:64-68). v5 deletes that guard and a test forbids bringing it back (tests/v5/test_conformance.py:363-366), even though v5 has never run on a free-threaded build (docs/v5/BLUEPRINT.md:192 marks this [U]). So a loud, known limit becomes an unverified claim.
concrete_risks_in_v5_code: src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:668 and :708: run_sleep_pass holds the global RLock across self._projector.project(), which in the compat path is author_stage_batch plus flush, i.e. layer.Save() (src/moneta/v5/compat.py:312-316). src/moneta/v5/usd/projection.py:31-57 does the same. Readers stall for the whole pass, every batch included. That walks back the section 15.6 narrow lock (ARCHITECTURE.md:312). Probe with a 50 ms/batch stand-in projector and 2000 staged records: the pass took 230 ms and recall's worst latency during it was 232 ms (in v1, query takes no lock).

src/moneta/v5/compat.py:141 (export_v1_snapshot) holds the substrate lock while it builds and JSON-encodes every recallable row plus vector, then writes and fsyncs. compat.py:531-534 calls it after every sleep pass, which is the SYNAPSE path. Probe: 10,000 records at dim 768 held the lock for 2,892 ms, so every SYNAPSE reader stalls about 3 s per pass at that size.

src/moneta/v5/journal.py:315-343 with substrate.py:425-427 and :643: every signal_attention is one fsync'd append under both the journal lock and the substrate RLock. Measured on Windows NTFS: 1,383 us per call with fsync and 10.9 us without, against 0.23 us for v1's append. That is about 6,000x. All writers (deposit and attend) are serialized, which caps total writes at roughly 700/s on this disk. Recall p99 rose from 0.30 ms to 2.5 ms with one concurrent attention writer.

The journal grows without bound and has no checkpoint. Every attend is a permanent line, and open replays the whole history (substrate.py:312). compact() (substrate.py:910-940) only strips erased payloads. Probe with 200 records: 10k attend events gave 1.2 MB and a 0.05 s reopen; 100k gave 11 MB and a 0.44 s reopen, growing linearly. v1 drains its log (attention_log.py:82) and truncates the WAL at snapshot (durability.py:121-125).

Free-threaded safety is asserted, not tested. The GIL sentinel was removed and a test now forbids it (tests/v5/test_conformance.py:363-366). The only check is _lock._is_owned() under the GIL (test_review_regressions.py:215). Lock-free readers of shared state remain: Substrate.seq (substrate.py:392-393) and closed. The optional Rust dot seam was never exercised without the GIL. No free-threaded interpreter exists on this machine (C:/Python314 has no python3.14t.exe), so the claim cannot be verified here.

Windows code paths are marked '# pragma: no cover' (journal.py:144, :161, :176, :375-381). On Windows, rewrite() closes the live fd before os.replace, and directory fsync is a no-op (journal.py:175-177). A replace refused by an external handle (Defender, indexer, a SYNAPSE reader) is caught and the fd reopened, which is fine, but none of it is covered by tests. The SYNAPSE compat evidence is Linux-only (docs/v5/SYNAPSE_COMPAT.md:13).

Migration hazard I observed here: C:/Python314/Lib/site-packages/moneta is a stale non-editable install with no v5 in it. Without PYTHONPATH, tests/v5/test_conformance.py::test_i6_same_journal_same_answers_in_another_process and tests/v5/test_journal.py::test_second_process_is_refused fail with ModuleNotFoundError: moneta.v5. With PYTHONPATH=src all 131 pass, including the msvcrt cross-process lock test. Mixed v1/v5 interpreters (hython and the server Python) are exactly the case SYNAPSE_COMPAT.md says v5 refuses rather than merges.

Behavior change: attention is now visible to recall right away (substrate.py:643 folds it at append). Under v1, ranking stays stable until the sleep pass. SYNAPSE's suite passes on the facade, but no test pins either behavior, and no real SYNAPSE store has been migrated (SYNAPSE_COMPAT.md 'What this does not show').

Minor: the substrate lock is an RLock (substrate.py:298), and the projector is called while it is held. A projector that calls back into the substrate can mutate the fold while run_sleep_pass is iterating over its precomputed 'pending' list. No current projector does this, but nothing prevents it.
conditions_to_attach_if_ruled_for_v5: Narrow the lock before E3 closes: run projector.project / author_stage_batch / flush outside the substrate lock. Take the batch under the lock, project with no lock held, then append the 'consolidate' event under the lock. That restores the ARCHITECTURE.md section 15.6 envelope. Acceptance: recall p95 stall during a sleep pass with the real UsdTarget under hython at 500-prim batches is 30 ms or less, measured and not projected.

Move compat export_v1_snapshot off the lock: copy rows under the lock, then serialize, write and fsync outside it, or run it in the background. Acceptance: SYNAPSE-path reader stall per pass is 30 ms or less at 10k x 768.

Add a journal checkpoint (a folded-state snapshot keyed to seq, with replay from that point) or attend-event coalescing, so open time and file size stop growing linearly with attention history. Set and test a reopen budget, e.g. under 1 s at 1M events.

Benchmark and document the Windows fsync cost: signal_attention and deposit p50/p99 on NTFS with fsync=True. Either add group commit (several queued events per fsync) or record the roughly 700 writes/s ceiling as part of the operational envelope.

Before removing the GIL dependency from the spec, run tests/v5, including the M5 lock test and the native seam parity tests, on a free-threaded CPython 3.13t/3.14t build. Until that passes, keep E3's free-threaded claim marked [U] in ARCHITECTURE.md and log a warning instead of nothing under sys._is_gil_enabled() == False.

Amend ARCHITECTURE.md section 5.1 explicitly: attention is visible immediately, and 'lock-free' becomes 'one writer lock, total order'. Add a test that pins the new visibility semantics. Do not leave it as a silent behavior change.

Re-run the SYNAPSE swap on Windows under both plain CPython and hython against a copy of a real store (e.g. the 841-record one). Cut over every interpreter together and remove or upgrade stale site-packages installs such as C:/Python314/Lib/site-packages/moneta.
Fix v1's docstring defect regardless of the ruling: api.py:416-418 says each signal is fsync'd, but durability.py:149 only flushes.
recommendation: Accept E3 for v5. Make E3's closure depend on three blocking conditions: (1) take USD projection out from under the substrate lock, (2) move the compat snapshot export off the lock, and (3) add a journal checkpoint so reopen time is bounded. Each needs a measured acceptance number on Windows/hython. Treat free-threaded support as a separate claim that stays marked [U] until a 3.13t/3.14t CI run passes. The skeptic's case for v1 does not hold on correctness. v1's durable attention is flush-only and lock-taking (durability.py:144-149). It loses acknowledged signals on crash and cannot run without the GIL. The case does hold on reader latency. As written, v5 trades v1's zero-lock query for a global RLock that is held across USD Save (measured 232 ms) and the compat export (measured 2.9 s at 10k x 768). If E3 is ruled for v5 without the lock-scope conditions, the Phase 3 reader-stall envelope (ARCHITECTURE.md:312) is silently reopened. That would be its own section 9 trigger. ruling: E4 should be ruled for v5's semantics: prune becomes a tombstone, and a separate operator erase exists. It should not be ruled for v5's implementation as it stands. The case for v1 partly holds. It holds on footprint and read cost: in v5 nothing ever removes a record from the fold, so recall, sleep-pass and RAM cost grow with every memory ever deposited, not with the live set. ruling:
Half-life call: when the half-life changes, should it rewrite history on replay (v5) or apply only from the change forward (v1)? Skeptic verdict: PARTIALLY HOLDS. The case for forward-only holds on one point. It does not hold on determinism, and it is not really a v1-versus-v5 architecture question. What v5 does now is deterministic, and while no sleep pass has run it is fully reversible: reopen with the old value and every utility comes back bit-exact. But once a sleep pass runs, the change becomes irreversible. A plain config edit can wipe out the whole store, and setting the old value back does not undo it.

Probe (scratchpad .../hl/probe.py; ManualClock; 30 deposits over 45h; half-life changed from 24h to 1h, which is inside the allowed range in decay.py:34-35; one sleep pass at the moment of change):
- Result: 30/30 tombstoned.
- Forward-only at the same instant would have pruned 0/30.
- Reopening with 24h leaves all 30 tombstoned and 0 recallable. model.py:300-301 never lets a tombstone go back to live, and v5 has no untombstone operation.

The rewrite also only goes part way. Utilities are recomputed, but the journal's retain and consolidate decisions (model.py:307-314) are frozen facts. So after a change the journal holds lifecycle decisions that contradict the utilities it now reports.

Forward-only is not ruled out by the journal design. The fold could carry λ per event and rebase every anchor when it hits a half_life_change event. That is just as deterministic, does one O(N) pass per change, and keeps the journal self-describing. So the real choice is between two semantics on the v5 journal, not between v1 and v5.
strongest_case_for_v1: Under forward-only, a half-life change is an operational adjustment and does not rewrite memory. Each record keeps the utility it earned under the policy that was in force, and only future decay uses the new rate. A mistake (wrong units, a test fixture's value, a library default bump) therefore does damage in proportion to how long it stays live, not in proportion to the store's total age. v5's reinterpretation turns a single config value into a hidden retroactive input to an irreversible operation: the next sleep pass tombstones on the rewritten utilities, and v5 has no untombstone. v5 also treats its two global parameters inconsistently. The journal owns the dimension (compat.py:422-423: "An existing journal owns its dimension"), but the caller's config silently overrides the half-life, with only a log warning (substrate.py:328-337). That means the journal alone cannot reproduce state: the note event is informational, and the fold's λ always comes from config (substrate.py:311, model.py:344-348). Finally, the usual argument that reinterpretation is needed for determinism is false. A journaled change event can just as well carry forward-only rebase semantics, which v1 already approximates by writing back last_evaluated at every evaluation point (ecs.py:255-284).
concrete_risks_in_v5_code: src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:328-346 - any open whose Config.half_life_seconds differs from the journal's value rewrites history with only a _logger.warning, then appends a note. There is no opt-in flag and no refusal, so opening a store with a different config is itself a write that changes the semantics of everything already in it.

src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:170 + src/moneta/decay.py:31 - Config defaults half_life_seconds to DEFAULT_HALF_LIFE_SECONDS. Any opener that omits it (an inspection script, a REPL, a test harness) silently reinterprets a non-default store. If a future release changes the library default, every existing store gets rewritten on upgrade.

src/moneta/v5/model.py:293-302 together with substrate.py:674-680 - the first sleep pass after a shorter half-life prunes on the reinterpreted utilities. Tombstones are one-way: _set_status skips TOMBSTONED->LIVE, and no untombstone or restore API exists (grep of src/moneta/v5 finds none). Probe: 24h->1h, then one pass: 30/30 tombstoned; reverting to 24h: 0 recallable. Forward-only counterfactual: 0 pruned.

src/moneta/v5/model.py:189-194,280-290 / substrate.py:311 - the fold's λ comes from config, not from the journal. genesis and half_life_change only set fold.half_life_seconds (model.py:220-221, 347-348) and never change fold.lam. So the journal is not self-describing: replaying it under a different config gives different state, and the note cannot be used to reproduce what actually ran.

src/moneta/v5/model.py:307-317 - the rewrite is partial. retain, stage and consolidate decisions made under the old λ stay as recorded, while utilities are recomputed under the new λ. After a change, explain() and records() can report utilities that contradict the recorded reasons for a tombstone or stage (e.g. a record tombstoned for 'decay' now shows a utility well above 0.1).

src/moneta/v5/compat.py:600-619 - imported v1 rows carry anchors (u, last_evaluated) that already include decay under v1's λ. A later half-life change only rewrites their history after the import, which contradicts the 'utility = f(journal, λ)' framing in model.py:4-7 and BLUEPRINT.md:129.

src/moneta/usd_target.py:321 - consolidated prims author a utility Float at projection time. After a half-life change, the USD cold tier and the journal disagree on utility for every consolidated record, and nothing marks that divergence.

src/moneta/v5/substrate.py:338-346 - the note's t is clock.now(), with no check against the journal's last t. Repeated opens with alternating configs (two entrypoints or interpreters) append a note on each open. Probe: 2 notes after one change and one revert. Harmless to state, but the change log becomes noise.
tests/v5/test_review_regressions.py:147-160 - the only half-life-change test checks that the note is recorded. Nothing tests change -> sleep pass -> revert, the destructive path shown above.

SYNAPSE impact: /c/Users/User/SYNAPSE/python/synapse/memory/moneta_store.py:318-337 never sets half_life_seconds, so it always runs at the 6h default. There is no exposure today. The exposure is a Moneta default change, or a second SYNAPSE entrypoint that sets it. The APPROVE consent gate on synapse_sleep_pass (moneta_store.py:844-1010) shows an audit but does not show that a half-life change caused the prune list.

Windows and crash windows: nothing specific to half-life. The note is one atomic append under the msvcrt sidecar lock (journal.py:143-172). A crash before it lands just re-notes on the next open. Performance: rewriting costs nothing beyond the replay that always runs; forward-only would cost one O(N) rebase per change event.
conditions_to_attach_if_ruled_for_v5: The journal owns the half-life, as it already owns dim: fold.lam comes from genesis and later change events, never from Config. An open whose config differs from the journal's value raises, unless the caller passes an explicit opt-in such as Config(half_life_change='reinterpret'). That flag then appends the event. No more warn-and-continue (substrate.py:328-337).

A half-life change is an explicit, owner-authorised journaled operation (consistent with v7 BLUEPRINT_v7.md:283 G2-10 'owner-signed amend'), not a side effect of opening. Read-only opens (inspection, export) must never append it.

Every retain event records the half_life_seconds it was decided under, so lifecycle decisions stay auditable against the utilities in force at the time, and explain() can say 'tombstoned under λ_old'.

The first sleep pass after a half-life change is gated: it runs as a dry run returning the would-prune set, or it is capped, and it requires explicit confirmation if it would tombstone more than a set fraction of LIVE records. SYNAPSE's audit should name the half-life change as the cause.

Tombstones caused by a decay retain can be reversed until the E4 erase step, via an un-tombstone/restore event that is itself journaled. Alternatively, document plainly that a half-life change followed by one pass is irreversible.
Changing DEFAULT_HALF_LIFE_SECONDS in a release must not rewrite existing stores (it follows from the genesis-pinned value above), and the release notes must say so.

Document the partial reach of the rewrite: retain and consolidate decisions are frozen, imported v1 anchors keep v1-λ decay up to their import point, and USD-authored utility values (usd_target.py:321) are not rewritten.

Add tests: change -> pass -> revert (the 30/30 probe as a regression); open with the default config on a store with a non-default half-life must refuse; the journal replays identically without the original Config.

Leave a forward-only mode (rebase anchors at the change event) open as a per-change option. It is deterministic on the same journal and costs one O(N) rebase, so ruling for v5's journal does not require ruling for retroactive semantics.
recommendation: Rule for v5's journal-and-fold design, but do not accept 'changing the half-life reinterprets history' as it is implemented now. Ruling for v5 is justified: what v5 does is deterministic and replayable, and it can be undone right up until a sleep pass runs. Determinism was never the issue. What actually breaks is that a config value read on open silently feeds the one irreversible operation, the sleep pass. Ruling for v1 is also not needed, because forward-only can be expressed as a journaled rebase event inside v5. Attach the conditions: the journal owns λ; changing it requires explicit opt-in and owner authorisation; retain events record λ; the first pass after a change is gated or dry-run; tombstones are reversible until erase; plus the regression tests. v7 G2-10 (BLUEPRINT_v7.md:283) already treats the change as a 'held, history-writing' amend, which covers the authorisation condition, but its implementation has to replace substrate.py:328-346, not sit on top of it. Jev's 0.84 on this call is the weakest of the five, and its inputs came from v5's own blueprint. Read it as 'v5 direction, conditions unresolved', not as settled.
